blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Set out the main measures of monetary policy, trace how each works through the banking system, and weigh their strength and drawbacks.

blocks.heading: The three main measures
blocks.text: The first measure is changing interest rates: the central bank raises or lowers the rate at which it lends to commercial banks, which tend to move their loan and deposit rates the same way. The second is controlling the growth of the money supply: the central bank can sell government securities to banks, which pay from their reserves and then hold less to lend, or tighten the rules under which banks create new deposits through lending. The third is changing the foreign exchange rate: a central bank can buy its own currency with its foreign currency reserves, which tends to raise its price, or sell it, which tends to lower it. The Namibian dollar is tied one-for-one to the South African rand, so the Bank of Namibia uses this measure to hold that link steady; how exchange rates are set is developed in topic 6.3.

blocks.heading: A rate rise traced
blocks.text: Suppose the policy rate rises from 4% to 8%. Etosha Gate Lodge plans a N$150 000 kitchen extension on a bank loan: at 4% the yearly interest is 0.04 x N$150 000 = N$6 000, at 8% it is 0.08 x N$150 000 = N$12 000, so the lodge is likely to postpone. Households move the same way - dearer credit, better-rewarded saving - so borrowing falls, fewer new deposits are created, and the growth of the money supply slows.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: The chain traces a rate rise only, which the revised list of measures still contains; the added exchange-rate measure needs no change here.

blocks.heading: A change in the exchange rate traced
blocks.text: The third measure works on the price of the currency itself. Take an invented economy whose currency is the crown. Its central bank sells crowns and buys US dollars with them, adding to the supply of crowns on the foreign exchange market, and the exchange rate falls from 10 crowns = US$1 to 12 crowns = US$1. A bag of coffee its farmers sell for 1 200 crowns used to cost a foreign buyer 1 200 / 10 = US$120; it now costs 1 200 / 12 = US$100, so exports become cheaper abroad. A machine priced at US$50 used to cost a local firm 50 x 10 = 500 crowns; it now costs 50 x 12 = 600 crowns, so imports become dearer at home. A central bank that buys its own currency with its reserves does the reverse: the exchange rate rises, exports become dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home, which tends to hold down the prices of imported goods such as fuel. Switzerland's central bank used the measure between 2011 and 2015, selling Swiss francs to stop the franc rising further against the euro and hurting Swiss exporters. Namibia uses the measure differently: the Namibian dollar is held at one-for-one with the rand, so the Bank of Namibia does not change that rate, and against the US dollar the Namibian dollar moves with the rand.

blocks.heading: Monetary measures or supply-side measures?
blocks.text: The boundary: a monetary measure works on the price and quantity of money - interest rates, the money supply, the exchange rate; a supply-side measure works on the economy's capacity to produce. The test is to ask what the measure changes - the price of money, or what the economy can produce. A grant helping Kaoko Juice buy bottling equipment is supply-side; a policy-rate rise is monetary.

blocks.heading: Interest rates or tax rates?
blocks.text: Interest rates and tax rates are both rates, but they belong to different policies. An interest rate is the price of borrowed money: the central bank changes the rate at which it lends to commercial banks, and their loan and deposit rates tend to follow, so it is a monetary policy measure. A tax rate is the share of income or spending the government takes by law, set in its budget, so it is a fiscal policy measure (topic 4.3). To tell them apart, ask who sets the rate and who receives the payment: interest goes to a lender, tax goes to the government. Cutting a tax rate does not make borrowing cheaper; cutting interest rates does.

blocks.heading: Strength and drawbacks
blocks.text: The strength of interest-rate changes is reach: they work through the whole banking system at once, reaching households and firms across the economy within days. Their drawbacks are that the effects arrive with a delay, spending financed without bank credit responds less, and dearer borrowing may hold back firms' building projects and jobs. A rate rise cools credit-financed spending faster than a cash-only market stall, in Vietnam as in Namibia.
